sweep_summary: Dutch (dutc1256) is in the catalog as weight-hedged, deciding source Taalportaal (Köhnlein 2015) summarising Kager 1989 and Booij 1995. Of the 43 title-hits, 11 concern Dutch word stress proper (van der Hulst 1984, Kager 1989, Kager 2000, Zonneveld 1993, Nouveau 1994, Neijt & van Heuven 1992, Trommelen/Zonneveld/van der Hulst 1999, Gussenhoven 1993, van Oostendorp 2012, Kager & Martínez-Paricio 2014/2018, de Bree & Wijnen 2016, plus Sluijter & van Heuven 1996 on acoustic correlates); the rest are intonation, sentence accent, phonetics, L2, verse metrics, dialect-attitude or Limburgian-dialect work. Read this sweep: Kager 1989 pp. 227-230 (major generalizations 'almost no exceptions': three-syllable window, schwa restriction, closed-penult restriction; minor ones with exceptions: superheavy final -> final, final VC -> antepenult, open final -> penult), van Oostendorp 2012 (critical review: penult default and superheavy/schwa effects robust, closed-penult weight evidence statistical with CELEX counterexamples -- the substance of the catalog's hedge), Kager 2000 (derived-word stress, assumes penult stem stress), and a new open copy of Kager & Martínez-Paricio 2018 (Linguistics 56: 69-114, Utrecht repository), whose p. 83 gives the cleanest one-paragraph statement (penult default; antepenult if penult open + final closed; final if superheavy; QS trochee). Two ISCA papers fetched sources (Sluijter & van Heuven 1996; Nota et al. 2016) are silent on placement. Everything read confirms or refines the existing coding; nothing contradicts it and nothing supersedes Taalportaal/Kager 1989 as deciding source. Not obtainable (De Gruyter/Brill bot-challenge, Benjamins paywall, Leiden/Radboud repositories blocked; 1999, Gussenhoven 1993 full text -- all medium priority, all expected to restate the same generalizations.

Some sub-patterns and lexical exceptions occur, which we will not discuss. Primary stress is penultimate ([a.'χa:.ta] 'Agatha'; [a.'mɑn.da] 'Amanda'), except in two cases: (a) in words of three or more syllables, primary stress is on the antepenult in case the penult is open and the final is closed (['ma:.ra.ˌtɔn] 'marathon'; ['ɑl.ma.ˌnɑk] 'almanac'); (b) primary stress is on the final if it is "superheavy" (CV:C or CVCC) ([to.'ma:t] 'tomato'; [ˌle.di.'kɑnt] 'bed').

sources.note: The Glottolog 2014 'Aspects of Germanic Phonology' entry corresponds to the 2018 Linguistics paper (Utrecht repository open copy, hdl 1874/396984). sources.quote: (12) When the penultimate syllable is heavy, stress cannot be on the antepenultimate. ... However, a CELEX search shows counterexamples for each of the classes in (14a) that are supposed to be impossible: (15) a. 'VC.VC.VC mangistan, badminton b. 'VC.VC.VV chimpanzee ... sources.note: Critical review: consensus is three-syllable window + quantity sensitivity, penult default, superheavy finals attract stress; argues the core heavy/light (closed-penult) evidence is statistical with CELEX counterexamples, while schwa-lightness and superheavy strength are robust; proposes Dutch is quality- rather than quantity-sensitive. Refines the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding by supplying the hedge's substance (KNAW open copy; also held in qs_tier record).
